newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl seeks SPD cooperation on tax, pension reform.
newsitem.headline: Kohl seeks SPD cooperation on tax, pension reform.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday appealed to the opposition Social Democrats to work with him to break a log jam on tax and pension reforms, predicting it would open the way for new investment and cut unemployment.

Speaking at a news conference alongside Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, the German chancellor said he was confident a proposed tax and pension reform programme would stimulate economic growth and create new jobs.
"In the coming weeks we want to push forward the tax reforms and seek out discussions with the opposition Social Democrats," Kohl said.
"I am certain that once we have a decision on tax reform that the atmosphere for investment will improve enormously."
Kohl has come under pressure to act after German unemployment reached a 64-year high of 12.2 percent in January, up by about a half a million from December to 4.66 million.
Kohl said the government never promised it would halve unemployment by the year 2000, but that this was a goal worth striving for.
"I do not see the slightest reason to abandon this objective," he said.
Kohl stressed that it was necessary to carry out the government's tax and pension reforms quickly to fight unemployment.

"Next week we will take steps to move forward on tax reform," he said. He appealed to all political parties for talks on the tax and pension plans, citing the need to lower the cost of labour as a key issue.
"We are prepared to talk with the Social Democrats and with other parties in order to reach a conclusion this year," he said.
Kohl said German must act now or run the risk of missing the Maastricht criteria needed for the country to qualify for the planned European monetary union in 1999.
A member of the government's independent economic council said record unemployment could force the government to make more budget cuts in order to meet the strict fiscal targets.

Rolf Peffekoven said in an interview with the daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung to be published on Saturday that Germany could miss the Maastricht limit of a three percent budget deficit to gross domestic product because of the surging unemployment.
"If the government wants to keep to its projected target of 2.9 percent, it would still have to achieve considerable savings in the current budget," Peffekoven said.
The independent council's projection of a 3.3 percent ratio was "more realistic," he said.
Kohl, asked if the higher unemployment would prevent Bonn from meeting the EMU criteria, said he was confident Germany would achieve the budget targets.
"I am certain we will do everything we can in order to meet the criteria, which we will do," he said. "To do this it is important that we carry out what we have already begun."
Prodi noted that the problem of unemployment was not limited to Germany or Italy alone. He said France, too, had more than 12 percent unemployment.
"This is a problem that is found throughout Europe," he said.
